Workstream · Q3 2026

Improve Activation Rate

Redesigning the agent-creation flow so more people who start building an agent actually finish.

70%
drop-off rate building agents
(higher for manual creation)
🧩 Problem

70% drop-off when building agents. Drop-off is higher when creating agents manually, vs. going through the AI Assistant.

🧪 Hypothesis

By rethinking the information architecture and prioritising mandatory steps, navigation, and guidance, we can reduce drop-off and help users build agents faster.

Source: Improve Activation Rate board, Figma

Multi-agent navigation

Problem: multi-artifact UX is confusing — no single anchor, users click back and forth between tabs trying to figure out the architecture.

Hypothesis: not settled yet — two different candidate directions, unvalidated:

H1 — clearer anchor/switching UI, keep the tab model

H2 — represent multiple in-progress agents as connected nodes on a canvas instead of tabs

Needs more evidence before picking one — e.g. a targeted Darwin question, or reviewing the recordings Sin referenced.

Not started

Agent-building loading states

Problem: the wireframe only shows the right panel (Model, Instructions, Capabilities, Triggers, Memory) fully populated. There's no illustrated state for while the AI Assistant is actively filling it in after the user describes what they want.

Hypothesis: not designed yet — something like a progressive checklist as each field gets filled in ("Researching tool availability ✓, Creating agent ✓, Adding tools ✓, Adding task ⋯"), similar to the pattern in the Notion "SEO Audit" reference screenshot.

Decisions

  1. 1Triggers moved before Capabilities in the section order — the agent gets triggered first, then its capabilities get used; order follows that sequence.Source: Giulio Andreini, video feedback
  2. 2Web search moves from Settings > Advanced into Capabilities.Team decision, Aug 2026 — resolves Open question 1 below
  3. 3Renamed "Run agent" → "Preview agent" — clearer term for what the action actually does (opens the preview chat).Team decision, Aug 2026 — supersedes the earlier "Run agent" rename in What changed #6
  4. 4Model stays prominent, near the top of the tab, even if it turns out to be auto-filled with a sensible default — a conscious, cost-relevant decision users should make deliberately either way.Source: Jan Ostrówka, Giulio Andreini, video feedback
  5. 5For now, ship the improved blocking tooltip when Instructions is empty — "Can't run agent yet," naming the actual consequence with one clear fix (see What changed #12) — rather than the fuller AI Assistant State 2 flow.
  6. 6Workflows are exposed as their own distinct capability, not buried in the flat "Add tool or skill" modal alongside MCP servers and native tools — a user looking for a workflow has a clear, separate path to find one.

Backlog

  1. 1Make the Preview-agent action a single, consistent, always-reachable affordance — currently reachable only via Triggers, not Capabilities. Reconcile into one spot (possibly a sticky top-bar action), repositioned to the top-right corner for better visual balance.Source: viewer comment; viewer 180e108e
  2. 2Reconsider the "*" required-field convention — unsure everyone understands it means "needed to run the agent."Source: viewer 180e108e
  3. 3When clicking Preview with empty Instructions, have the AI Assistant prompt the user to write instructions — but without offering a "test it anyway" escape hatch. Stricter than the current State 2 in the AI Assistant panel (What changed #14), which offers both "test it anyway" and "add quick instructions first": here, there's no option to test the agent without instructions at all.Source: Sim Superville, Giulio Andreini, video feedback

Open questions

  1. 2Should Sessions live as a small icon next to Run agent instead of being its own tab? Sessions is a log of past runs — arguably a byproduct of running the agent (exactly what Run agent triggers) rather than a peer configuration area like Knowledge or Settings. Not resolved.
  2. 4Should the Settings tab become a gear icon + modal instead of a full tab, since its contents (max parallel sub-agents, custom model routing, Advanced) are more secondary/infrequent than Build, Knowledge, or Sessions? Open risk: n8n's own left sidebar already uses a gear icon for account-level Settings, so a second one here could read as the same thing — and there's no evidence yet that today's Settings tab is itself a pain point. Aesthetic/structural idea, not evidence-backed so far.
  3. 6What do users actually type into Instructions? With Triggers below the fold, people might type trigger conditions directly into Instructions instead (e.g. "Every day at 9am, send me a Slack message giving me a motivational speech"). Could indicate users think in terms of an outcome/intent rather than separate fields — worth exploring whether Instructions and Triggers should combine into a more natural-language-first experience, where the AI Assistant structures the user's intent into the right components.Source: feedback via Slack thread (Rob); reasoning extended by Martina
  4. 7"Channels" vs. "Triggers" as the section name — one reviewer prefers "Channels" over the current "Triggers" label. Not reconciled.Source: viewer comment
  5. ✓Should Web search live under Capabilities instead of Settings > Advanced? It's arguably another thing the agent can use, same as a Tool. One reason it might belong where it is instead: cost — each web search call is plausibly billed per use, unlike attaching a Tool or Workflow, which has no per-use cost surfaced here. Resolved — see Decision #2.
  6. ✓"Add tool or skill" opens a modal that mixes MCP servers, n8n native tools, n8n nodes, and Workflows under one flat list (99+ MCP entries alone) — a user looking specifically for an n8n workflow has no clear, separate path to find one. Resolved — see Decision #6.Source: Add tool modal screenshot, Aug 25
  7. ✓Is Model actually auto-filled with a sensible default for new users? It's currently kept at the top on the assumption that it isn't (a required-but-empty field is a real risk). Resolved — see Decision #4: Model stays at the top even if it turns out to be auto-filled.

What changed

  1. 1Tab at top — likely exists for switching between agents the AI Assistant creates in one session. Not fixed here — see Multi-agent navigation (not started).Source: Sin sync notes, Aug 21
  2. 2Model + Instructions grouped at the top, ahead of Tools/Triggers. The "default model selected" banner is replaced with a compact Default badge next to the model name — same reassurance, far less vertical space. Model stays required and visible up top rather than being demoted, since it isn't auto-filled for new users (see Open questions).
  3. 3Instructions placeholder replaced with a worked example, matching the pattern already decided for the AI Agent node's Input field.
  4. 4The real screen has a single "+ Add tool or skill" action with Sub-agents tucked in as a second line beneath it. Here, Tools, Workflows, Skills, and Sub-agents are four peer rows inside one "Capabilities" box (see #19) — each with its own icon and add-action, not flattened into one list. Matches how Notion keeps its sub-agent equivalent ("Notion agents") as a distinct row alongside Web access/Notion inside one "Tools and access" box, rather than a separate section. Workflows also gets its own row so it's discoverable on the Agent tab itself, independent of whatever the Add-tool modal itself does (see Open questions).Source: n8n "Build and manage agents" doc; Notion Tools-and-access UI
  5. 5Add channel now matches the plain-row style used for Tools & Skills, instead of a dashed callout box — there was no reason for it to look like a different kind of action.
  6. 6Renamed Preview → Run agent, matching Notion's exact term for the same action. Kept as its own pill-button subsection at the top of Triggers, separated from the channel/schedule rows below by the same divider convention used throughout — its position alone signals it works with zero channels configured, no explanatory sentence needed.Source: Notion agent Triggers UI; AGENT-692 preview drop-off
  7. 7Memory brought onto the Agent tab instead of staying buried in Settings — it's a bigger lever on agent behavior than its previous placement suggested.Source: Darwin answers; AGENT-597
  8. 8Sections grouped into four boxed cards (Model & Instructions / Capabilities / Triggers / Memory — Memory kept as its own card rather than folded into Triggers) instead of one long list — mirrors the boxed-card pattern already used on the real Settings tab, so the Agent tab reads consistently with the rest of the product.
  9. 9AI Assistant welcome state replaced the bare "Ask anything" prompt with a short intro + example prompts, styled distinctly from the Instructions placeholder so the two don't read as the same example shown twice. Subtitle copy also spells out that the assistant builds and configures the agent (model, instructions, tools) on the user's behalf, not just chats about it — the example chips alone don't make that obvious.
  10. 11Added a required-field asterisk to Model and Instructions — the only two fields an agent can't run without — matching how the real "Add skill" modal already marks its own required fields.Source: Add skill modal screenshot, Aug 25
  11. 12Reworded the run-blocked error tooltip: "Can't run agent yet" names the actual consequence instead of the generic "This agent's configuration has errors," and the fix is one plain sentence ("Add instructions describing what this agent should do") instead of a colon lead-in plus a one-item bullet list. This is still the fallback/blocking version, though — the ideal version doesn't block Run agent at all: let it run, and have the AI Assistant prompt the user to add instructions instead. See State 2 in the AI Assistant panel for that flow.Source: Preview error tooltip screenshot, Aug 25
  12. 13Sessions empty state now explains what fills it: "Sessions will appear here after you run your agent" instead of a bare "No agent sessions" with no next step, and it names the actual action ("run your agent") to match the Run agent button.Source: content-design pass, Aug 25
  13. 14The real AI Assistant panel just shows an empty "Ask anything" input with no response to clicking Run agent without instructions. Here, the panel has two explicitly labeled states, switchable with the ‹ › arrows above it — State 1 (empty) and State 2 (after clicking Run agent with no instructions, where the assistant offers test it anyway or add quick instructions first instead of just blocking). Modeled directly on Notion's own agent chat, which does exactly this when its Instructions page is empty.Source: Notion agent chat screenshot, Aug 25
  14. 15Removed the left sidepanel-toggle icon from the tab bar — redundant with the full-screen expand icon already sitting on the right of the same row, and it wasn't doing a distinct job.
  15. 16Vector stores sits under Advanced, inside Knowledge — not promoted to its own always-visible box, and not moved to Settings > Advanced either. It genuinely is a rare/technical setting (connecting a pre-indexed external store), but its *category* is still knowledge grounding, the same job as file upload — Settings > Advanced is about model/execution behavior (web search, reasoning, concurrency), a different concern entirely. Splitting "where does this agent get its knowledge" across two tabs would be worse than just collapsing the rarer path behind a disclosure within Knowledge. n8n's own product direction reinforces this: internal notes describe wanting vector stores usable "without needing deep technical knowledge," i.e. abstracted away for most users, not surfaced as an equal, default-visible option.Source: Notion "Easy Vector Store" notes
  16. 18Renamed the first tab Agent → Build — "Agent" just repeated the object's own name, unlike Knowledge/Sessions/Settings, which each name a category of content. "Build" names what actually happens on this tab instead.
  17. 19Renamed "Tools & Skills" → "Capabilities" — the box now holds four rows (Tools, Workflows, Skills, Sub-agents), and the old name only described two of them.
  18. 20The Instructions formatting toolbar is no longer always visible — it now appears as a floating popover only when text is selected (double-click a word, or drag-select a range), and disappears once the selection is cleared. A persistent 15-icon bar was disproportionate chrome for what is fundamentally a system-prompt field.

Preview and Navigation

Two problems with how Preview, Assistant, and Trace coexist across the Agent builder and Agent view. A full clickable prototype, a stress-test critiquing it, and a refined version with those cuts applied — all below.

First analysis Floating panel on Agents Embedded panel on Agents

Problem 1

Users can't navigate Agent view in an easy, predictable way. Root cause: layout mode selection doubles as a functionality switch — choosing a display option (Docked / Full screen / Open in new tab) silently decides what's even available, rather than being a purely visual choice.

Three symptoms, same root cause. While actively in Preview, there's no way to reach the AI Assistant at all — you have to leave Preview first, because that layout mode hides it. Opening an existing agent (the "Molly" case, via Loom) landed a user on the config page with no guidance toward Sessions, even though they were there to check on activity, not configure anything. And whether Preview shows by default at all currently depends on which layout mode was last selected, not on why someone opened the agent — the layout choice is deciding the functionality, not just the display.

Problem 2

The same controls invert depending on where you are. Full screen (and other options) do different, sometimes opposite things in Agent builder versus Agent view. This also breaks an established platform pattern: elsewhere in n8n, the sidepanel icon means "expand/collapse this panel." Here it's been repurposed to mean "change layout mode" instead — so the same icon now carries two different jobs depending on where you encounter it.

Current navigation — the real product, as observed

Not the proposal — this is what exists today, reconstructed from the screenshots and Loom feedback reviewed throughout this workstream. It's here to make Problems 1 and 2 concrete: layout mode hides functionality (Problem 1), and the same "sidepanel" icon means something different in Agent builder than it does in Agent view (Problem 2) — with dead ends and no way back either way.

Approach 2 — the stress-test cuts applied

Same two clickable prototypes as Approach 1, with the redundant and weak-case controls the stress-test flagged actually removed rather than just noted. Nothing here is untested speculation — every cut traces back to a specific dot above.

Assumptions this proposal rests on

Each cut below relies on a belief about what users actually need — stated here so it can be checked against real data later, not just accepted because it sounds reasonable.

  1. Assumption: Preview being always visible when viewing an existing agent is useful to users. → Decision: no Preview on/off toggle in Agent view; it just always shows.
  2. Assumption: Users rarely need the AI Assistant chat to fill the whole frame. → Decision: no dedicated Full screen control for Assistant, in Builder or Agent view.
  3. Assumption: In Agent builder, closing Assistant already gives Settings all the room it needs. → Decision: no separate "full-screen Settings" in Builder — the Assistant toggle already gets you there.
  4. Assumption: A brand-new, unconfigured agent has no meaningful conversation history yet. → Decision: no chat-history icon in Builder's Assistant panel.
  5. Assumption: In Agent view, when Assistant and Preview are both open, users still want a fast way to focus on Settings alone. → Decision: Settings keeps its Full screen control here — the one case that survived the stress-test.

← Workstreams
Workstream · not started

Power-user productivity

For people who already know the product and want to move faster — a different persona and a different goal than Activation Rate.

🧩 Problem

Experienced users have no fast path through things they already know how to do — keyboard shortcuts, starting from a blank agent instead of the AI-Assistant flow, and moving an agent's definition in/out of n8n (import/export).

🧪 Hypothesis

Not settled yet. These items were originally raised as candidates for Improve Activation Rate, then scoped out: they serve returning users who are already past the point of dropping off, not first-time builders. Test before adding anything here: does this help someone succeed at their first build, or does it help someone already capable move faster? If the latter, it belongs in this workstream, not Activation Rate.

Screens
Screens land here as this workstream gets scoped
(e.g. a "create blank" entry point, an import/export flow, a shortcuts overlay)
← Workstreams
Workstream · In progress

Goal-based tasks

Giving agents the ability to pursue a goal across time instead of running one-shot — a different foundation layer than Activation Rate or Power-user productivity.

TBD
session completion rate
(goal met vs. abandoned / cost-capped)
TBD
requests judged complex enough
to go goal-based
🧩 Problem

Agents in n8n today are one-shot — they run when triggered, hold no state across time, and can't pursue a multi-step goal to completion. Community users hit this ceiling when they try to build agents that pursue outcomes over hours or days, and either fall back to workflow patterns stitched together with manual "wait" nodes, or go to competitors that already support this.

🧪 Hypothesis

By giving agents a state substrate, goal/plan tracking, and execution mechanics (checkpointing, resume, clean termination on completion or cost cap), we can let agents pursue a goal across time and survive interruptions — driving community adoption of goal-based agents.

Source: Notion — "Long-running goal-based agents" (Agents team, Q3 2026 roadmap)

About this step

← Goal-based tasks

Goal-based task flows and wireframes

Original proposal Revised proposal Draft

What is a long-running task?

Simple test: is the agent just running a fixed script when something triggers it, or is it actually chasing an open goal it has to keep judging its own progress on?

What it is
  • Waits in between — short bursts of work, waiting on a person or event in between. Takes a long time overall, but the agent isn't actually busy most of that time. Example: a support-triage agent sitting on a channel for days.
  • Working non-stop — lots of steps back to back, no waiting, genuinely busy the whole way through. Example: deep research, or "find 500 leads and add the good fits to HubSpot."
What it is not
  • Short, scheduled or triggered — nothing to wait for. Example: today's Slack Agents Digest — checks hourly, posts or stays quiet. Looks like monitoring, but it's really just a fixed routine, not a real goal.

How this works, in a nutshell

Before the roles, the risk rules, and the screens below — the whole thing as a flow.

1
Identify & plan
Set up ahead of time by the author, or spotted on the fly when a request is too big for one reply — either way, the agent puts together a plan and shows it, skipped for simple, obviously-scoped prompts.
→
2
Approve
In chat, you approve the plan before it starts. Triggered any other way — schedule, API, Slack — it skips that and only asks when something risky comes up.
→
3
Work it
Check in, pause, edit, or leave it running in the background — anything genuinely risky still gets a check with you first, unless the author already said not to ask.
→
4
Done, plainly
Eventually it finishes, and tells you plainly what it did.

Proposed flow

Two entry intents, one shared execution path — combining the Notion PRD's author/user split with the FigJam sketch. Explicit: the mode is turned on deliberately — by the author ahead of time, or anyone via the + menu in Preview. Implicit: the agent proposes going long-running itself when a prompt is complex enough.

    LRTE1["Mode picked
deliberately"]
  end

  subgraph LRT_IMP["Implicit — during use"]
    LRTI1["User describes

    LRTI2 -->|"Simple"| LRTI3["One-shot reply"]
    LRTI2 -->|"Complex"| LRTI4["Agent proposes

  end

  LRTE1 --> LRTG["Goal captured"]

Author vs. consumer Use cases map Stopping, pausing, and failing Session status, at a glance Explicit invocation, elsewhere

Author vs. consumer — who can do what

Follows Design principle #1 and #2 above: the author defines the ceiling and the risk categories once; the consumer operates a session within them.

Author can

Builds and owns the agent — configures it, sets its limits, and can also use it like a consumer would.

  • Turn on Long-running task mode for the agent at build time (the explicit path)
  • Define which actions count as low-risk vs. high-risk for this agent
  • Set the cost cap (overall and per session) and the autonomy ceiling
  • Edit the agent's plan-generation instructions
  • Choose the default approval-channel routing
  • Test the agent themselves via Preview — acting as a consumer would, but with full configuration rights
  • View the trace/progress of any session
Not in MVP
  • Grant or withhold auto-mode for consumers, up to the ceiling they define
Consumer can

Uses an already-published agent — triggers and steers a session, but never past what the author configured.

  • Trigger a long-running task, explicit or implicit, within what the author published
  • Start the generated plan for their own session
  • Request plan changes conversationally (re-plan via feedback) — not structurally edit it
  • Pause, resume, or cancel their own session
  • Choose to be more conservative than the author's default (ask about more things) — never more permissive
  • View the trace/progress of their own session

Use cases map

Sync channel (chat / Preview — human likely present) Async channel (Slack, schedule, API — human may be absent)
Author, explicit trigger Configures a long-running mode in Agent builder, tests it in Preview themselves
E.g. turns on Long-running task mode for "Sales Outreach," then types the leads request into Preview to try it.		 Configures it, then it runs on a schedule/cron without them watching
E.g. same toggle, but invoked by a weekly schedule instead — the author never types anything, just checks Sessions later.
Author, implicit trigger Their own complex prompt — at the start of a chat or partway through — gets proposed as long-running Unlikely — an implicit proposal needs someone present to respond to it
Consumer, explicit trigger Invokes an already-built long-running mode via a chat channel, stays present Triggers it via a non-chat channel (Slack command, API) without staying
Consumer, implicit trigger Their own complex ask gets proposed as long-running, they approve live Hardest case: mid-run, the agent needs a decision but no one's there — this is what's driving the auto-mode, guardrail, and cost-cap questions

Explicit invocation, elsewhere

Evidence for Open question #4 below — how today's research agents decide whether to go long-running, and whether the person has to ask for it by name.

Product How you invoke it Can it propose itself? Plan shown before it runs Access
ChatGPT "/deepresearch", the + tools menu, or the sidebar Not for Deep Research itself — but the base model still auto-escalates reasoning effort (and can reach for its own lighter web search) on a hard prompt, without turning into this specific agentic pipeline Yes — picks sources (web, files, connected apps), reviews a plan, then builds the report Plus, Team, Enterprise, Pro
Gemini Add Files → Deep Research, in the composer No — explicit only Yes — editable plan, then "Start research" Gemini Apps (web + mobile)
Perplexity Pick "Deep Research" from the mode options before sending No — explicit only Not surfaced as a separate step Free: very limited daily · Pro: ~20/month (cut from ~500–600/month in Feb 2026)
Claude No in-composer toggle — a Settings-level Research Mode selector (Standard / Enhanced / Deep Research), set generally rather than per message, or just asking in plain language ("please use the research tool") Yes — can activate itself for a qualifying query, unprompted Not surfaced as a separate approval step Max, Team, Enterprise
GitHub Copilot Session mode dropdown below the prompt field — Interactive / Plan / Autopilot, changeable any time No — explicit only, all three modes Only in Plan mode — creates a plan first, you review and approve before it executes. Interactive asks step by step instead (no upfront plan); Autopilot skips both and just runs. Copilot agent sessions (Free, Pro & Team per current docs)

Not a clean match either way. n8n's implicit path (agent judges complexity, proposes it itself) is the one Claude alone also does. n8n's explicit path — a picker inside the composer, via + — is closer to ChatGPT/Gemini/Perplexity's pattern instead: Claude has no per-message, in-composer toggle at all, only a Settings-level mode or asking in plain language. So the proposed n8n flow doesn't map cleanly onto any single competitor — it borrows the explicit UI pattern from three of them and the self-initiating behavior from the fourth. One caveat on ChatGPT's cell above: "not for Deep Research itself" is scoped to that one tool — the base model still adapts to a hard prompt on its own, it just doesn't escalate into this particular multi-step, cited-report pipeline unless asked. GitHub Copilot adds a third pattern: not a single toggle but three explicit modes on a spectrum (no plan → plan → full autonomy), still always user-picked, never proposed by the agent. Seeded from a quick scan on 2026-08-31 — add rows as you find more.

Session status, at a glance

Every state a session can be in, and what it looks like — referenced throughout the prototypes below (MVP decision #10).

StateLookMeans
Running RunningActively executing steps. Can be paused, or left running in the background.
Needs approval● Needs approvalBlocked on one risky action. Nothing else proceeds until it's approved or rejected.
Paused● PausedStopped by request. Resumes exactly where it left off — nothing is lost.
Completed✓ CompletedGoal met, halted cleanly. Trace and summary stay available afterward.
Cancelled✕ CancelledEnded for good, not resumable — different from Paused.
Failed✕ FailedA tool call itself errored (API failure, timeout) — not a normal pause point like Needs approval. Retry picks the same step back up.

Stopping, pausing, and failing — elsewhere

Evidence for the open question below. None of these ship true pause-and-resume of a single in-flight run — only Stop/Cancel (permanent) and, in some cases, a live redirect that doesn't actually stop the run.

ProductStop / CancelRedirect while still runningTrue pause + resumeNotes
ChatGPTYes — only way to redirect if it's off track"Update" — inject context without stoppingNo—
GeminiYesNot offered for a single queryNo for a single run — Pause/Resume exists only for recurring Spark schedules, a different thing—
Claude CodeYes (Ctrl+C)Interrupt, then "continue"No — open feature request; background sessions currently die on pause, don't resume—
GitHub Copilot CLIYes (Esc/Ctrl+C)Rollback undoes committed changes — not the same as resumingNo — open feature request—
Perplexity Labs / Computer TasksYes, explicitly permanentNot offeredNo"Needs attention" groups blocked jobs; transient failures retry automatically a few times

Confirms the pattern: Cancel is universal, a live in-flight redirect is common, true pause+resume is not.

About this view

Same trace, as nodes instead of a list — closer to the Darwin tracing exploration. Branching, not a line: two subtasks can run side by side, and a node waiting on approval is a real state here too. Click a node to see what's happening inside it.

Autonomy and risk

Two halves of one model: the rules (Design principles) and what they mean concretely in n8n (Risky vs. not risky, below) — read together, not as separate topics.

🛡 Design principles

Ground rules for every decision below — referenced rather than re-argued each time a screen or setting touches autonomy or risk.

  1. A consumer session can never exceed the autonomy ceiling the author configured for risky actions — it can only be more conservative (ask about more things), never more permissive.
  2. What counts as low-risk vs. high-risk for a given agent is defined once by the author, at build time — not something each consumer configures per session.
  3. Non-chat/async invocation paths (schedule, workflow, API) default to per-tool approval. Full autonomy on these paths is an explicit, author-granted exception, never a silent default.
  4. Some actions stay gated no matter what mode or ceiling is active — real spend beyond the cap, and irreversible external actions (see "Risky vs. not risky" below).

Risky vs. not risky, in n8n

Grounds Design principle #2 and #4 in concrete n8n actions, not abstract risk levels.

Not risky — safe to pre-approve
  • Reading or searching data (CRM lookup, database read, workflow read)
  • Searching the web
  • Reading or summarizing files
  • Drafting a message or report without sending or publishing it
  • Checking the status of a system
  • Internal calculations or analysis
Risky — always confirm, or capped by the author's ceiling

Not risky as a manual n8n action — sending a Slack message is completely routine when a person or a configured workflow does it. It's risky specifically when the agent decides on its own, mid-run, to do it.

  • Sending a message externally (Slack, email, SMS) to a real recipient, on the agent's own judgment
  • Executing a payment or financial transaction
  • Deleting or overwriting production data
  • Publishing or deploying a workflow or agent
  • Modifying a live credential, webhook, or integration
  • Calling a third-party API with a real side effect (creating a ticket, canceling a subscription, updating a customer record)
  • Posting publicly

MVP decisions

  1. 1The plan is generated and surfaced by default; approval is required to start, for the chat-invoked path.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  2. 2Non-chat/async invocation (workflow, API, cron) proceeds straight to execution with per-tool HITL instead of an upfront plan approval — already the flow above.
  3. 3Plan changes happen conversationally — user gives feedback in a textarea, the agent re-plans and re-shows it — not through a separate structured plan editor.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  4. 4Progress shows as step-based framing ("3 of 7 steps"), not a calendar-time estimate — agents can't reliably predict duration.Source: comment thread, Aug 28 (rejects the literal hours/weeks ask)
  5. 5Approval granularity ships as four primitives: Approve all always / Approve once / Cancel / Per tool.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  6. 6Those primitives are bundled into a few named presets for the author (e.g. "Ask before everything" / "Ask only for risky actions" / "Don't ask, just notify"), with per-tool as an advanced option — not a flat grid by default.
  7. 7Cost cap exists at both agent level (overall) and session level; author-only editable, with a notify-me option.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  8. 8Approval defaults to the channel the task was triggered in.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  9. 9Short and long-running tasks get distinct visual treatment — a persistent status pill for the long-running one vs. an ephemeral indicator for a short reply.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  10. 10Status states cover at least: running, paused, completed.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  11. 11Users can pause and resume a long-running task. Kept even though no major competitor researched ships true pause-and-resume of a single in-flight run — the Needs-approval case is why it still earns its place: other subtasks can be genuinely running in parallel while one thing is blocked on approval, so pausing everything is a real, distinct action from approving or rejecting that one item. Resolves former Open question #6.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  12. 12The agent stays conversationally available for quick questions while a long-running task executes in the background — the chat input isn't locked to the long-running session.Source: viewer 6966e30d
  13. 13Tool-call/error visibility reuses the existing Trace view, extended with the long-running-specific elements already sketched (goal header, subtask groups) — not a new surface built from scratch.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  14. 14"Invoke via chat" is dropped as a separate concept; both flow-diagram branches use the same "Preview" label.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  15. 15The consumer can request plan changes conversationally, same mechanism as the author (Decision #3) — not an author-only capability. Resolves former Open question #6.

Not in MVP

  1. 1Per-channel cost cap granularity (e.g. different caps for Slack vs. Web vs. Telegram) — agent- and session-level caps cover the common case for now.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  2. 2Consumer-level auto-mode and its guardrails — what happens if a consumer wants zero interruptions, and what the cost implications are. Real question, deferred until the core approval loop (MVP decisions above) is proven.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  3. 3Configurable approval-channel override — routing approvals to a channel different from where the task was triggered (e.g. running on web, approving via Slack).Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  4. 4Multiple concurrent long-running sessions for the same agent and channel, from different users — not the main use case per the original scoping note.
  5. 5The hardest use-case cell from the map above — consumer, implicit trigger, async/no-one-present — needs the consumer auto-mode and guardrail work (item 2) resolved first.
  6. 6Actual default values for the Settings screen (which options are pre-selected, what the edit-icon modal contains) — the mechanism is scoped, the specific defaults aren't chosen yet.Source: comment thread, Aug 28
  7. 7A fully explicit "Don't ask me anything" option distinct from "Approve all always" — revisit once real usage shows the existing primitive isn't enough.Source: comment thread, Aug 28

Open questions

  1. 1Why is the main use case framed around Preview rather than Agent builder — is it really "build a complex agent" vs. "execute a complex agent," and does that split hold up?Source: raised on the FigJam board, not yet answered in the Notion PRD
  2. 2Can a user have multiple goals / sessions running at once, and if so, is that a single composite goal decomposed into sub-goals, or genuinely parallel sessions?Source: raised in Notion PRD comments
  3. 3Does Slack (or any channel medium) get an explicit trigger at all, given it has no textarea mode picker — or is it implicit-only there?
  4. 4Is the explicit "Long-running task" picker actually needed, or could we rely entirely on the agent detecting goal complexity and proposing it itself? The explicit option adds a second path to design and maintain — worth it only if it's doing a real job beyond letting users discover the capability exists. Is discoverability itself that job, or is there more to it?
  5. 5Could the graph/canvas view (screen 7, currently "vision, not P0") actually be the release UI instead of the timeline + session list — skip the phased build and show progress as nodes from day one? Would need to weigh against the PRD's own reasoning for deferring it (P0 ships on existing surfaces to keep scope small).

What changed, and why

  1. 1No more explicit invocation path — no author toggle, no "+" picker in the composer. The model alone judges whether a request needs to become a goal-based session, every time.Source: Bakery feedback (Nik, Giulio) — resolves former Open question #4
  2. 2A plan is no longer guaranteed. Some goals get one to approve; others are simple enough that the agent just starts working. Either way, approval still happens whenever a plan exists.Source: Bakery feedback — Nik: "the plan keeps changing to fit the goal"; Giulio: "plan and long-running don't go together"
  3. 3A plan isn't fixed once approved — new steps can surface hours or days later as the agent learns more. The agent says this upfront, so it isn't a surprise later.
  4. 4Trace is graph nodes by default now, not a phased future addition — resolves former Open question #5. The kanban variant is dropped.Source: Bakery feedback — Tuukka: kanban isn't a native n8n visualization
  5. 5Each node shows the agent's reasoning for that step, not just which tool it called.Source: Bakery feedback (Sim)
  6. 6Mid-run checkpoints are visible in the trace, and a session can restart from one instead of the very beginning.Source: Bakery feedback (Aniol)
  7. 7Visibility is designed for two states, not one — live while you're watching, and catching up on everything that happened while you were away.

How this works now

One path, not two — the model decides on its own whether a request needs to go goal-based, and whether it needs a plan. Replaces the Explicit/Implicit split in the original proposal.

a goal"] --> C{"Model judges

  C -->|"Simple"| O["One-shot reply"]
  C -->|"Complex"| G["Goal captured"]
  G --> P{"Needs a
plan?"}
  P -->|"No"| X["Executing"]
  P -->|"Yes"| PL["Plan proposed
(may grow later)"]

resume / restart
from checkpoint"| X
  X --> D["Goal met —
halts cleanly"]

How this works, in a nutshell

1
Judge, maybe plan
The agent alone decides if a request needs to go goal-based, and if it needs a plan at all. Simple, obviously-scoped requests skip both.
→
2
Approve, if there's a plan
Shown before it starts, flagged as something that may change — not a fixed contract. Skipped entirely if no plan was needed.
→
3
Work it, visibly
Graph nodes show progress and reasoning, not just tool calls. Checkpoints let you restart partway through, not just from the beginning.
→
4
Done, plainly
Finishes and tells you what it did — the full trace stays available afterward, whether you watched it happen or not.

Brought over from the Original proposal, with one addition: a fourth column showing the state in actual motion, grounded in n8n's own real motion system (n8n-io/n8n-design-system — motion.scss: spin, pulse-glow, fade-in). Not every state gets animation — stillness is deliberate for the ones that are already settled.

StateLookMeansIn motion
Running Running Actively executing steps. Can be paused, or left running in the background. real spin mixin
Needs approval ● Needs approval Blocked on one risky action. Nothing else proceeds until it's approved or rejected. real pulse-glow — used by N8nPulse for exactly this "needs you" signal
Paused ● Paused Stopped by request. Resumes exactly where it left off — nothing is lost. no motion — stillness reads as paused
Completed ✓ Completed Goal met, halted cleanly. Trace and summary stay available afterward. ✓ real fade-in — eases in once, doesn't loop
Cancelled ✕ Cancelled Ended for good, not resumable — different from Paused. no motion — a terminal state, nothing left to draw attention to
Failed ✕ Failed A tool call itself errored (API failure, timeout) — not a normal pause point like Needs approval. Retry picks the same step back up. no motion — the red pill itself already draws the eye; looping it would nag

What changed, and why

  1. 1No more explicit invocation path — no author toggle, no "+" picker in the composer. The model alone judges whether a request needs to become a goal-based session, every time.Source: Bakery feedback (Nik, Giulio) — resolves former Open question #4
  2. 2A plan is no longer guaranteed. Some goals get one to approve; others are simple enough that the agent just starts working. Either way, approval still happens whenever a plan exists.Source: Bakery feedback — Nik: "the plan keeps changing to fit the goal"; Giulio: "plan and long-running don't go together"
  3. 3A plan isn't fixed once approved — new steps can surface hours or days later as the agent learns more. The agent says this upfront, so it isn't a surprise later.
  4. 4Trace is graph nodes by default now, not a phased future addition — resolves former Open question #5. The kanban variant is dropped.Source: Bakery feedback — Tuukka: kanban isn't a native n8n visualization
  5. 5Each node shows the agent's reasoning for that step, not just which tool it called.Source: Bakery feedback (Sim)
  6. 6Mid-run checkpoints are visible in the trace, and a session can restart from one instead of the very beginning.Source: Bakery feedback (Aniol)
  7. 7Visibility is designed for two states, not one — live while you're watching, and catching up on everything that happened while you were away.

How this works now

One path, not two — the model decides on its own whether a request needs to go goal-based, and whether it needs a plan. Replaces the Explicit/Implicit split in the original proposal.

flowchart LR
  U["User describes
a goal"] --> C{"Model judges
complexity"}
  C -->|"Simple"| O["One-shot reply"]
  C -->|"Complex"| G["Goal captured"]
  G --> P{"Needs a
plan?"}
  P -->|"No"| X["Executing"]
  P -->|"Yes"| PL["Plan proposed
(may grow later)"]
  PL --> APR["User approves"]
  APR --> X
  X --> R["Progress viewable anytime
live, or after the fact"]
  R -->|"Pause / edit /
resume / restart
from checkpoint"| X
  X --> D["Goal met —
halts cleanly"]

How this works, in a nutshell

1
Judge, maybe plan
The agent alone decides if a request needs to go goal-based, and if it needs a plan at all. Simple, obviously-scoped requests skip both.
→
2
Approve, if there's a plan
Shown before it starts, flagged as something that may change — not a fixed contract. Skipped entirely if no plan was needed.
→
3
Work it, visibly
Graph nodes show progress and reasoning, not just tool calls. Checkpoints let you restart partway through, not just from the beginning.
→
4
Done, plainly
Finishes and tells you what it did — the full trace stays available afterward, whether you watched it happen or not.

Two ways of watching it happen

Same session, different context — live in the platform, or catching up after being away.

While you're here
  • The graph updates live, node by node
  • Approval prompts appear inline the moment they're needed
  • Pause, edit the plan, or restart from a checkpoint at any time
When you're not
  • Progress posts as it happens in the channel it was triggered from — not a silent background process
  • You're notified only when it needs you, or when it's done
  • Opening the trace afterward shows the same graph, with everything that happened while you were away

Approval mode, in detail

The full picture behind the compact picker in Agent Author's Settings below — MVP decision #6's named presets, each grounded in what it actually changes for the consumer.

Ask before everything

Every tool call needs approval, every time — including the "not risky" ones below. Highest oversight, slowest to run unattended. Good fit while an agent is new and unproven.

Ask only for risky actions — default

Only actions on the "Risky" list below need approval (sending outreach emails, spending money, publishing, etc.). Everything else runs without asking. The balance most agents should ship with.

Don't ask, just notify

Runs fully autonomous, notifies after the fact instead of asking first. Real spend beyond the cost cap and irreversible actions still always ask (Design principle #4) — this mode can't override those hard gates.

Per tool — advanced

Set approval on or off for each tool individually — the same list as "Risky vs. not risky" below, one row at a time. For when a preset doesn't quite fit this agent.

For reference — GitHub Copilot's own session modes
  • Interactive: you and the agent work together — it suggests changes and waits for your input before proceeding.
  • Plan: the agent creates a plan first. You review and approve the plan before it executes.
  • Autopilot: the agent works fully autonomously, without waiting for input.
